metadata.title: Identifying the optimal predictors for adolescent mental and physical health using machine learning methods

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 as a secondary dataset and restricts the analytic sample to 15-year-old students from Hong Kong and the Netherlands after excluding cases with missing values. The manuscript does not report using PISA sampling weights or any replicate-weight scheme, and it does not name any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or describe complex-survey variance estimation. Because the models are implemented in Python and the paper focuses on predictive performance (RMSE and R²) with repeated train/test splits, the analysis likely proceeds without explicit complex-survey weighting, which can affect generalizability and uncertainty quantification under clustered sampling. The main preprocessing steps explicitly described are one-hot encoding for categorical predictors and z-standardization fitted on the training set and applied to the test set to reduce leakage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 microdata and focused on 15-year-old students from Hong Kong and the Netherlands. The original sample comprised 5907 students in Hong Kong and 5046 in the Netherlands; the final analytic sample included only cases after removing missing values (no imputation was used). The study then retained 46 shared predictors across nine domains (parental domain removed) and applied one-hot encoding for categorical predictors. For model evaluation, each repetition used a 7:3 train/test split within each society, with z-standardization parameters estimated on the training set and applied to the test set.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Friend contact via phone or social media
Time since last outing with friends
Feelings when with friends: full of energy

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Grade 9/15-year-old Mental health (psychosomatic symptoms, 6-month frequency items)
top_predictors: Ease of communication about worries and concerns (SOCCON)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Within-society (Netherlands): RMSE 0.571–0.583, R² 0.417–0.429. Within-society (Hong Kong): RMSE 0.692–0.713, R² 0.287–0.308. Cross-society (NLD→HKG): RMSE 0.699–0.723, R² 0.277–0.301; (HKG→NLD): RMSE 0.595–0.637, R² 0.363–0.405.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Grade 9/15-year-old mental health the study leveraged emotional control, ease of communication about worries, and stress resistance (with additional social-capital and physical-domain predictors depending on society) to predict students’ average psychosomatic symptom frequency, finding that models achieved higher predictive fit in the Netherlands than in Hong Kong (R² about 0.42 vs. 0.29) and that cross-society generalization was weaker than within-society prediction. This indicates that emotional regulation and communication-related supports may be high-priority targets for adolescent mental-health interventions, while cultural context should be considered because predictor–outcome relationships do not transfer equally across societies, and the study is predictive (not causal).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Grade 9/15-year-old Physical health (self-rated health item)
main_findings.target_variable: Physical health (reserved self-rated health score; higher=better)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Within-society (Netherlands): RMSE 0.780–0.824, R² 0.176–0.220. Within-society (Hong Kong): RMSE 0.817–0.861, R² 0.139–0.183. Cross-society (NLD→HKG): RMSE 0.851–0.871, R² 0.129–0.149; (HKG→NLD): RMSE 0.785–0.833, R² 0.167–0.215.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Grade 9/15-year-old physical health the study leveraged body image and social connection to parents as shared key predictors (and, depending on society, feeling safe and stress resistance) to predict students’ self-rated physical health, finding that predictive performance was consistently lower for physical health than for mental health (R² roughly 0.14–0.22) and that within-society models outperformed cross-society models. This indicates that interventions targeting body-image-related concerns and supportive parent–adolescent connections may help physical-health outcomes, but improvements may require locally tailored components because cultural/ecological differences appear to moderate which predictors matter most, and the evidence remains correlational/predictive rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzed PISA 2022 microdata for 15-year-old students from Hong Kong (n=3253 after listwise deletion) and the Netherlands (n=2781), predicting two adolescent health outcomes using repeated 7:3 train/test splits and feature selection. Mental health was operationalized as the average of nine psychosomatic symptom frequency items (higher score = poorer mental health), while physical health used a single self-rated health item (higher score = better physical health). Across both societies, the best-performing predictive models achieved higher fit for mental health than physical health: in the Netherlands, mental health R² ranged 0.417–0.429 (RMSE 0.571–0.583) versus physical health R² 0.176–0.220 (RMSE 0.780–0.824). Cross-society generalization was weaker than within-society prediction, with Netherlands→Hong Kong R² for mental health 0.277–0.301 and for physical health 0.129–0.149. The paper does not report using PISA sampling/replicate weights and uses listwise deletion without imputation, so uncertainty and generalizability may be affected; additionally, feature importance and predictive accuracy do not establish causal effects.
